source.title: Block Recursive Transformers for Structured Parameter Sharing
source.authors: José Marques; Hyunyoung A. Cho; Youngeun Kim; You-Jia Zhang; Aecheon Jung; Kyuhong Shim; Sungeun Hong

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a Kaplan et al. scaling-law compute estimate to estimate training FLOPs, but does not test the loss-scaling laws or fit scaling exponents.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation NLL across compute budgets, comparing parameter-sharing architectures, but does not test whether the loss follows a power law or whether smaller runs predict larger runs. Its downstream-accuracy results and NLL comparisons for other architectures do not test the listed scaling claims.
record.test_reason: The paper uses the Kaplan et al. (2020) FLOPs estimate only to place runs on a compute axis. It compares recursive parameter-sharing topologies. It fits no power law, tests no extrapolation, does not study compute-optimal allocation, and does not test predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss. The NLL comparisons at three compute budgets (Figure 3) report only how its own method ranks against baselines. The token sweeps (Figure 4) do the same.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Block Recursive Transformers improve validation NLL and downstream accuracy over static recursive-sharing baselines, across model scales, data budgets, recursion settings and architecture types. They also conclude that intermediate block granularity is a key design factor.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not fit or test the original scaling laws; it studies recursive parameter-sharing topologies and uses a Kaplan et al. scaling-law compute estimate to estimate training FLOPs.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relative NLL gains are more pronounced at recursion count R = 4 than at R = 2; the paper also compares results across compute budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: For SmolLM-360M, BRT has the lowest validation NLL among static sharing strategies at all three estimated compute budgets, for both R = 2 and R = 4. The gap is larger at R = 4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recursive weight-sharing topology (block granularity) changes language-model loss at matched unique-parameter count and compute.

fits_no_version.finding: At a matched 157M unique parameters and 10B tokens, final training loss is 3.41 for BRT, 3.48 for Middle-Cycle and 3.70 for Middle-Sequence (Figure 9). T5 and ModernBERT NLL also differ by sharing topology (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How shared layers are organised across depth affects loss in parameter-shared Transformers, which the unique-parameter count alone does not capture.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The compute-budget NLL results are presented in a figure without exact values or stated uncertainty, and the study does not fit or evaluate power-law scaling relationships.
record.rows_left_out: No other results included: the downstream-accuracy comparisons and the encoder-decoder and encoder-only NLL comparisons concern sharing-strategy performance, not a tested scaling-law version.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Only three compute budgets, shown in a figure.
No fit on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.

Depth and width shape of standard Transformers at fixed parameter count is not varied. The topology comparisons concern recursive weight sharing, where executed depth and compute differ from untied models.
T5 and ModernBERT NLL are reported at a single 10B-token budget, with no scaling fit.
Downstream accuracy is reported at 1B–20B tokens and at 135M–1.7B parameters, but predictability from scale or loss is not analysed.
No fitted exponents and no comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's guesses (uses_without_test, T4, no labels) are confirmed. The only link to the scaling-law literature is the Kaplan FLOPs estimate used for the x-axis of Figure 3. Excluding the downstream and encoder results from rows is appropriate. They could be added as fits_no_version context, but no version-bearing result is omitted.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test power-law relationships between held-out loss and parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Does not fit laws on small runs or test predictions on larger runs.
Does not determine or compare compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
Does not test how architecture details affect loss at fixed parameter count in the sense of this version.
Does not test power-law scaling in other modalities or the listed training regimes.
Reports downstream accuracy under different sharing strategies and training-token budgets, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
Does not examine dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, or whether scaling curves bend.
